paper.abstract.v3: A replication with a local model ({v3_setup.reviewer_model_name}) on {v3_local.complete_triples:int} instances finds intent recovery of {v3_local.tests.intent_all.floor:pct} without clarification, {v3_local.tests.intent_all.treatment:pct} with it and {v3_local.tests.intent_all.ceiling:pct} with full context. Gap recovery was {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}), not significant, and the upper limit rules out recovering more than a third of the gap. Re-scoring with the agent judge preserved this verdict but not the effect size.
paper.intro.contrib5: a judge-calibration analysis of AI-vs-AI agreement across three AI judges, and a replication on a local reviewer that is reported separately from the original study.
paper.sys.extraction: using the Python AST for Python and tree-sitter grammars for JavaScript, TypeScript/TSX, Java, C, C++ and Rust, with Python behaviour byte-identical to before
paper.sys.backends: Three provider backends sit behind one interface: Gemini, Anthropic and local Ollama. The Ollama backend runs a model on the user's own machine, with no key, no traffic beyond that machine and no monetary cost.
paper.sys.bot: Parked runs persist in SQLite across restarts, a timeout sweep publishes reviews that go unanswered, rate limits are handled, and signed webhooks are verified. The bot passes offline end-to-end tests and has also been run on live GitHub in a sandbox repository, as described below.
paper.live.demo: A demonstration, not an evaluation: {live_demo.n_prs:int} constructed pull requests in the authors' sandbox repository. On the first, reviewed from the command line, the detector asked (score {live_demo.pr1.score:f2}, threshold {live_demo.pr1.threshold:f2}) and the author confirmed that the removed email check was intentional, raising the reviewer's confidence from {live_demo.pr1.without_answer.overall_confidence:pct} to {live_demo.pr1.overall_confidence:pct}; the verdict was {live_demo.pr1.verdict}. On the second, reviewed by the webhook bot behind a tunnel, the answer showed that removing the disabled-account check was unintended, and the bot requested changes with {live_demo.pr2.n_findings:int} {live_demo.pr2.finding_severity} {live_demo.pr2.finding_category} finding. The bot retried through {live_demo.pr2.facts.provider_retries:int} transient provider errors. The run used a laptop, a free-tier quota and a heuristic detector, so it estimates no rate or effect.
paper.method.v3_design: The replication uses {v3_design.rows:int} rows: the {v3_design.v2_rows:int} rows of the original set plus {v3_design.n_new_rows:int} new rows. The set includes all {v3_design.mutants_used:int} verified mutants, scored in both arms, and {v3_design.golden_only_rows:int} golden-only rows from {v3_design.golden_only_repos:int} other repositories. The reviewer was {v3_setup.reviewer_model_name}, served through Ollama, with the heuristic detector at τ = {v3_setup.threshold:f2}. The {v3_setup.runs:int} runs had {v3_setup.runs_failed:int} failures and took {v3_setup.wall_minutes:int} minutes on a laptop GPU. The question and oracle model was {v3_setup.question_oracle_model}, whose identity is recorded in the oracle log but not per database row. Conditions were the same as in the original study. The replication is never pooled with the original study, and the judge is chosen in Section V-G rather than here.
paper.results.v3_lead: Table III reports the same measures as Table I for the local reviewer {v3_setup.reviewer_model_name}, served through Ollama, with outcomes scored by the Claude agent judge {v3_local.judge_label}. That judge was chosen after seeing its agreement with the local judge, as explained in Section V-G. The replication is reported separately from the original study and is never pooled with it.
paper.results.v3_effect: Clarification did not significantly recover intent in the replication. Over {v3_local.tests.intent_all.n:int} instances, intent recovery was {v3_local.tests.intent_all.floor:pct} without clarification, {v3_local.tests.intent_all.treatment:pct} with it and {v3_local.tests.intent_all.ceiling:pct} with full context. Gap recovery was {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}, McNemar p = {v3_local.tests.intent_all.mcnemar_p:f2}), not significant. The upper limit of the interval rules out recovering more than about a third of the gap at this sample size. The manipulation works: withholding intent cost {derived.v3_local.intent_all.gap_points:int} points of intent recovery against full context, and clarification restored {derived.v3_local.intent_all.treatment_points:int} of those points. By subset, gap recovery was {v3_local.tests.intent_golden.gap_recovery:f2} on the golden rows (p = {v3_local.tests.intent_golden.mcnemar_p:f2}) and {v3_local.tests.intent_mutant.gap_recovery:f2} on the mutants (p = {v3_local.tests.intent_mutant.mcnemar_p:f2}), neither significant.
paper.results.v3_funnel: Detector recall was the limit, as in the original study. The detector asked on {v3_local.treatment_asks:int} of {v3_local.treatment_n:int} treatment reviews. Of the {v3_local.funnel.floor_misses:int} changes that the reviewer misread without clarification, the detector asked on {v3_local.funnel.detector_asked:int} and missed {derived.v3_detector_missed:int}. The simulated author answered {v3_local.funnel.author_answered:int} of those {v3_local.funnel.detector_asked:int} questions, and the treatment recovered intent on {v3_local.funnel.treatment_recovered:int} of the {v3_local.funnel.floor_misses:int} changes. Effects went in both directions: clarification helped on {v3_local.tests.intent_all.discordant_treatment_better:int} instances and hurt on {v3_local.tests.intent_all.discordant_floor_better:int}. Once a question was answered, the treatment recovered intent in {v3_local.funnel.treatment_recovered:int} of {v3_local.funnel.author_answered:int} cases, so most of the loss lies in deciding when to ask. Recall, not the answer, is the limit.
paper.results.v3_defects: Defect detection stays near the floor even with full context. The mutant rows caught the injected defect on {derived.v3_local.defect_mutant.floor_k:int} of {v3_local.tests.defect_mutant.n:int} without clarification, {derived.v3_local.defect_mutant.treatment_k:int} with it and {derived.v3_local.defect_mutant.ceiling_k:int} with full context ({v3_local.tests.defect_mutant.floor:pct}, {v3_local.tests.defect_mutant.treatment:pct} and {v3_local.tests.defect_mutant.ceiling:pct}; McNemar p = {v3_local.tests.defect_mutant.mcnemar_p:f2}). A small local reviewer, {v3_setup.reviewer_model_name}, limits defect detection, as in the original study. Over {v3_local.tests.false_alarm_golden.n:int} golden rows, false alarms were {derived.v3_local.false_alarm_golden.floor_k:int} without clarification, {derived.v3_local.false_alarm_golden.treatment_k:int} with it and {derived.v3_local.false_alarm_golden.ceiling_k:int} with full context, too few to separate the conditions (p = {v3_local.tests.false_alarm_golden.mcnemar_p:f2}). The study makes no claim about an effect on defects.
paper.results.judges_lead: Three AI judges scored the original reviews: the API judge {judges.models.api_v2}, Claude Sonnet agents ({v3_local.judge_label}), and the {judges.models.gemini_web} on a stratified sample of {judges.gemini_sample.n:int} runs, stratified by condition and variant. Table IV gives percent agreement, kappa and n for each judge pair. All of this is AI-vs-AI agreement, not validation against human scorers.
paper.results.judges_v2: Against the agent judge, the API judge agreed almost perfectly on defects (kappa {judges.v2_pairs.api_vs_agent.defect_caught.kappa:f2}, {judges.v2_pairs.api_vs_agent.defect_caught.percent_agreement:pct} agreement, n = {judges.v2_pairs.api_vs_agent.defect_caught.n:int}) and on false alarms (kappa {judges.v2_pairs.api_vs_agent.false_alarm.kappa:f2}), and was {judges.v2_pairs.api_vs_agent.intent_recovered.reading} on intent (kappa {judges.v2_pairs.api_vs_agent.intent_recovered.kappa:f2}, {judges.v2_pairs.api_vs_agent.intent_recovered.percent_agreement:pct} agreement, n = {judges.v2_pairs.api_vs_agent.intent_recovered.n:int}). The Gemini web app agreed with the agent judge on intent at kappa {judges.v2_pairs.gemini_vs_agent.intent_recovered.kappa:f2}, and the three judges agreed on intent for {judges.v2_three_way_intent.all_agree:int} of {judges.v2_three_way_intent.n:int} runs. Re-scoring the original study with the agent judge gave intent floor {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.floor:pct}, treatment {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.treatment:pct} and ceiling {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.ceiling:pct}, and gap recovery {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}, McNemar p = {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.mcnemar_p:f2}). The verdict holds: the effect is not significant. The size of gap recovery does not: under the API judge it was {v2.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v2.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}). paper.results.judges_v3: In the replication, the local judge, {v3_local_llama_judge.judge_model}, is unusable: its agreement with the agent judge was {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.intent_recovered.reading} on intent (kappa {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.intent_recovered.kappa:f2}, {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.intent_recovered.percent_agreement:pct}, n = {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.intent_recovered.n:int}), {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.defect_caught.reading} on defects (kappa {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.defect_caught.kappa:f2}) and {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.false_alarm.reading} on false alarms (kappa {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.false_alarm.kappa:f2}). It never flagged a false alarm (total {v3_local_llama_judge.false_alarm_total:int}) and wrote that no defect was injected on {v3_local_llama_judge.no_defect_claim_mutant.k:int} of {v3_local_llama_judge.no_defect_claim_mutant.n:int} mutant rows ({derived.llama_no_defect_claim_pct:int}%). The Claude agent judge {v3_local.judge_label} is therefore the primary judge for the replication. That choice was made after seeing the agreement figures, so it is a post hoc choice. paper.disc.replication: Two reviewers and two judge configurations give the same qualitative picture: recall is the binding limit, defect detection is limited by the reviewer, and no gap-recovery interval excludes zero. The size of the effect depends on which judge scores the reviews. In the original study, gap recovery was {v2.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} under the API judge (interval {v2.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}) and {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} under the agent judge (interval {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}). In the replication, under the agent judge, it was {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}) on {v3_local.tests.intent_all.n:int} instances. The sign of the effect is therefore not established under any of these judges, and magnitudes should be read together with the judge that produced them.
paper.threats.v3: The replication adds further limits. Both studies have small samples: the original has {v2.complete_triples:int} instances and the replication {v3_local.complete_triples:int}, so intervals are wide. The agent judge was chosen after seeing its agreement with the local judge, which makes the choice post hoc. The question and oracle model is small, and its identity is recorded in the oracle log but not per database row. The studies differ in reviewer and judge as well as in rows, and they are never pooled. A single review per condition cannot separate the effect from the reviewer's own run-to-run variation. The live GitHub demonstration covers {live_demo.n_prs:int} constructed pull requests in the authors' own sandbox repository, run from a laptop behind a tunnel; it shows that the loop works but estimates nothing. Live deployment on real third-party pull requests is not done, and the {realpr.n_prs:int} collected real pull requests are not yet labelled.
paper.conclusion.v3: A second reviewer, a small local model, and a second judge reproduce the null result: gap recovery was {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}, McNemar p = {v3_local.tests.intent_all.mcnemar_p:f2}), not significant, and its upper limit rules out recovering more than about a third of the gap. The effect size depends on the judge.
report.abstract.v3: A local-model replication finds gap recovery of {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}), not significant, and its size depends on the AI judge. Also added: multi-language support, an Ollama backend and a GitHub bot, demonstrated live in a sandbox repository. Not done: real-PR labelling, a human check of the replication's judges, permanent hosting and runs on third-party pull requests at scale.
report.s1_3.scope: The project builds a pull request reviewer that detects ambiguous intent and asks the author before commenting. The system analyses Python repositories and, through tree-sitter grammars, JavaScript, TypeScript/TSX, Java, C, C++ and Rust, with Python behaviour unchanged. It is delivered as a GitHub bot that responds to pull request webhooks, and it is restricted to the four stages described in Chapter 4. An editor extension and any interface beyond pull request comments remain out of scope. Permanent hosting, runs on real third-party pull requests at scale and the human studies are pending rather than out of scope. The bot has been demonstrated live on a sandbox repository (Section 6.4), and the {realpr.n_prs:int} collected real pull requests are not yet labelled.
report.s1_3.eval_scope: The evaluation covers two studies that are never pooled. The original study used free-tier hosted models on {v2.complete_triples:int} instances. The replication used a local model, {v3_setup.reviewer_model_name}, served through Ollama, on {v3_design.rows:int} rows, in {v3_setup.wall_minutes:int} minutes on a laptop GPU. The project also provides tooling for a paired developer study (Study B), which has not been run. A field deployment is not attempted, which is why the target is technology readiness level four.
report.s3_2_2.economic: The original study ran on the Google Gemini free tier at zero monetary cost (Section 7.7). Its binding constraint was a per-day request quota applied per model; the design accommodated it by assigning roles to different models, committing results per instance and resuming after a reset. The original study used {v2_tokens.input:k} input and {v2_tokens.output:k} output tokens. The replication ran through Ollama with {v3_setup.reviewer_model_name} on a laptop GPU, at zero monetary cost, in {v3_setup.wall_minutes:int} minutes. No hardware, licence or dataset was purchased; all libraries are open source.
report.s5_1_1.extraction: The semantic layer parses the post-change file, using the Python AST for Python and tree-sitter grammars for JavaScript, TypeScript/TSX, Java, C, C++ and Rust, and maps each changed line to its enclosing function, method or class, recording whether the signature changed; the Python path is unchanged.
report.s5_1_4.ollama: The Ollama backend calls a local model over HTTP and records the model name and digest that actually served each call. It needs no key, no connection beyond the local machine and no monetary cost.
report.s5_1_5.bot: The bot is built to keep working under the conditions a live deployment meets. Parked runs, those waiting for an author's answer, are stored durably in SQLite, so a restart resumes them. A timeout sweep publishes a review when the author does not answer in time. Rate limits are handled, signed webhooks are verified, and duplicate deliveries are handled. The bot passes offline end-to-end tests, within a suite of {derived.tests_passed:int} passing tests ({derived.tests_skipped:int} skipped) across {test_files:int} files. It has also run against live GitHub in a sandbox repository, as Section 6.4 reports. Permanent hosting and use on third-party pull requests are not done.
report.s5_2_5.calibration: The judge-calibration analysis gives the same context and instructions, blind to condition, to three AI judges: the API judge {judges.models.api_v2}, Claude Sonnet agent judges ({v3_local.judge_label}), and, on a stratified sample of {judges.gemini_sample.n:int} reviews, the {judges.models.gemini_web}. A local judge, {judges.models.api_v3}, scored the replication. Agreement between judges is reported as percent agreement and Cohen's kappa for each of the three checklist questions (intent recovered, defect caught and false alarm), and the study is re-analysed under each judge, so that every effect estimate can be read against the judge that produced it. This is AI-vs-AI agreement, not validation against human scorers.

These comparisons are AI-vs-AI agreement, not validation against human scorers.
report.s7_9.v3: In the replication, the local judge, {v3_local_llama_judge.judge_model}, is unusable: its agreement with the agent judge was {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.intent_recovered.reading} on intent (kappa {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.intent_recovered.kappa:f2}, {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.intent_recovered.percent_agreement:pct}, n = {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.intent_recovered.n:int}), {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.defect_caught.reading} on defects (kappa {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.defect_caught.kappa:f2}) and {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.false_alarm.reading} on false alarms (kappa {judges.v3_pairs.llama_vs_agent.false_alarm.kappa:f2}). It never flagged a false alarm (total {v3_local_llama_judge.false_alarm_total:int}) and wrote that no defect was injected on {v3_local_llama_judge.no_defect_claim_mutant.k:int} of {v3_local_llama_judge.no_defect_claim_mutant.n:int} mutant rows ({derived.llama_no_defect_claim_pct:int}%). The Claude agent judge {v3_local.judge_label} is therefore the primary judge for the replication. That choice was made after seeing the agreement figures, so it is a post hoc choice. The local judge's own intent result, gap recovery {v3_local_llama_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local_llama_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}), is reference only, and its intent recovery across the three conditions was {v3_local_llama_judge.tests.intent_all.floor:pct}, {v3_local_llama_judge.tests.intent_all.treatment:pct} and {v3_local_llama_judge.tests.intent_all.ceiling:pct}. All of this is AI-vs-AI agreement. Only the original study's API judge has been checked against human scorers, as reported in Section 7.11; the replication's judges have not.
report.s7_9.robust: Figure 7.7 plots gap recovery with its interval under four combinations: the original study with the API judge and with the agent judge, and the replication with the agent judge and with the local judge, whose interval is hatched because that judge is unreliable. The size of gap recovery depends on the judge, but every interval reaches zero: {v2.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v2.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}) under the API judge, {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v2_agent_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}) under the agent judge, {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}) for the replication under the agent judge, and {v3_local_llama_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local_llama_judge.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}) under the local judge. The judges should not be ranked by which gives the better gap recovery.
report.s7_10.post_hoc: The replication's judge, {v3_local.judge_label}, was chosen after seeing its agreement with the local judge, which was unusable, so the choice is post hoc and is disclosed as such.
report.s7_10.oracle: The question and oracle model, {v3_setup.question_oracle_model}, is small, and its identity is recorded only in the oracle log, not in each database row, so its effect on the results cannot be checked row by row.
report.s7_10.new_rows: The local replication differs from the original study in reviewer and judge as well as in its {v3_design.n_new_rows:int} added rows, so the two are never pooled; the full set's run on the original reviewer is reported separately, as a check on reviewer variance.
report.s7_10.bot: The GitHub demonstration (Section 6.4) is {live_demo.n_prs:int} constructed pull requests in the authors' sandbox repository, run from a laptop behind a tunnel on a free-tier quota. It shows the loop works, is not an evaluation, and leaves behaviour on third-party pull requests at scale untested.
report.conclusion.v3: The replication on a local reviewer and the judge calibration give a null result with a bound. Over {v3_local.tests.intent_all.n:int} instances, gap recovery was {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_recovery:f2} (interval {v3_local.tests.intent_all.gap_ci:ci}), not significant, and its upper limit rules out recovering more than about a third of the gap. The judge calibration is AI-vs-AI agreement, and the effect size depends on the judge, so each magnitude holds only under the judge that scored it. The original and replication studies are never pooled. Not done: a human check of the replication's judges, labelling of the {realpr.n_prs:int} real pull requests collected from {realpr.n_repos:int} repositories, the developer study (Study B), and permanent hosting with a run on real third-party pull requests at scale. The bot has been demonstrated live on {live_demo.n_prs:int} sandbox pull requests, which is not an evaluation.
deck.demo.live: The loop ran on live GitHub for {live_demo.n_prs:int} sandbox pull requests, from the command line and the webhook bot, and the answer changed the review (verdict {live_demo.pr2.verdict} on the second). A demonstration, not an evaluation.
